subject: Accounting
title: How Sales Tax Works
description: A short lesson to help you apply How Sales Tax Works.

hook.text: The price tag says $10 but you pay $10.88. That extra 88 cents is sales tax.

buildup.text: Sales tax is charged at the point of purchase, collected by the seller, and sent to the government.

discovery.text: Rates vary wildly—from 0% in Oregon to over 10% in parts of Louisiana when state and local combine.

twist.text: Five U.S. states have no sales tax at all: Oregon, Montana, New Hampshire, Delaware, and Alaska.

climax.text: Sales tax is simple to collect but hits lower-income earners harder—they spend more of their pay.

punchline.text: Everyone pays the same rate. Not everyone feels it equally.

quiz.question: Why is sales tax considered regressive?
options: It takes a larger percentage of lower incomes
It only applies to luxury goods

details.summary: Sales tax is a consumption tax collected at the point of purchase, where retailers add a percentage to the sale price and remit it to the government. It is the primary tax revenue source for most U.S. state and local governments.
details.whyItMatters: Sales tax affects virtually every purchase consumers make and is the financial backbone of state and local government services, making it one of the most widely encountered taxes in daily life.
takeaways: Sales tax is collected by retailers at the point of sale and remitted to state and local governments
Rates vary widely by state and locality, ranging from 0% to over 10% in some areas
Most states exempt essentials like groceries and medicine from sales tax

faq.question: How does sales tax work?
faq.answer: When you buy a taxable item, the retailer adds the applicable sales tax percentage to the price. The retailer collects this tax from customers and periodically remits it to the state and local governments. The retailer acts as a collection agent — the tax is on the consumer, not the business.

faq.question: Why do sales tax rates vary so much across the United States?
faq.answer: Each state sets its own sales tax rate (five states have none at all), and many allow cities and counties to add their own local taxes on top. This creates a patchwork where combined rates can range from 0% in Oregon to over 10% in parts of Louisiana, Tennessee, and Arkansas.
